title: Routing bandwidth vs quantization sensitivity
content:
Summary:
This is an exploratory runbook + notes dump investigating how quantization choices interact with MoE routing and long-context workloads to change effective bandwidth (PCIe/NVLink) and observable end-to-end latency. Goal: find patterns that explain when quantization helps vs when it regresses when routing (expert selection/scatter-gather) and long KV lifetimes dominate GPU memory behavior.

High-level hypothesis: quantization reduces model memory footprint and kernel compute time but can increase scatter/gather overhead because dequant/pack/unpack steps and additional host<->device transfers (when experts are remote) can dominate. The net perf depends on: (a) hardware topology (NVLink vs PCIe-only), (b) expert placement/replication strategy, (c) whether attention and KV-cache paths are quantized natively or are still FP16 hot paths, and (d) sequence length distribution.

What we ran (experiment matrix):
- Models: Llama-2-70B-v2-Chat (MoE partitioned variant used for internal routing tests), Mistral-Instruct-7B, Qwen-14B.
- MoE configs: top-k routing k=1/2, capacity_factor=1.0/1.5, expert_replication=1/2.
- Context lengths: 2k, 16k, 32k, 64k.
- Quantization: fp16 baseline, 8-bit dynamic (AWQ-like), int8 inference kernels, q4_0/q4_1 (LLM.int8-style), mixed where attention stays fp16 and feedforward is quantized.
- Hardware: 4x A100-80GB with NVLink (mesh), 8x A100 (PCIe-only rack) and single-node H100-80GB for microbenchmarks.
- Batch sizes: 1 (latency SLO), 8 (throughput), 32 (stress).
- Metrics captured: p50/p90/p95 latency, tokens/s, GPU memory usage, PCIe/NVLink transfer rates (nvlink-smi and nvidia-smi stats), kernel-level timings (Nsight/trace), memcpy timings, GPU occupancy, and host CPU stall fractions.

Profiling methodology notes:
- Use Nsight Systems for end-to-end traces; capture memcpy and kernel events to correlate large memcpy spikes with routing/reshard points.
- Instrument routing code to emit route_time and scatter_gather_time counters per request.
- Add simple per-expert serialization time counters (dequant + memcpy to expert device).
- For long-context traces, tag traces with average key length and observe KV-cache copy sizes.

Top-level findings (short):
1) On NVLink-enabled multi-GPU systems, quantization tends to help more consistently — reduced DRAM working set means fewer cross-device page migrations and fewer large NVLink transfers during KV prefetch. Result: 8-bit yields ~8–16% lower p95 for 32k context on replicated-expert setups compared to fp16 in our runs.
2) On PCIe-only racks (no NVLink), quantization sometimes regresses latency for MoE configs where experts live on different PCIe-connected hosts because the dequant+serialize step forces extra host-side buffering and synchronous memcpy, increasing p95 by 10–30% at batch=1 for 16k+ contexts.
3) Mixed quantization (only FFN quantized, attention fp16) was the best compromise for long-context workloads: attention kernels dominate KV memory movement; quantizing FFN reduced GPU memory and improved token/s while avoiding extra roundtrips during attention paths.
4) Routing policy matters: top-1 routing (fewer experts touched) benefits more from quantization than top-2 routing which amplifies scatter overhead; at top-2 we saw an extra 12–25% scatter_gather_time compared to top-1 for same quant config.
5) Expert replication reduces remote memcpy but increases peak memory; with replication=2 on NVLink setups, quantization+replication produced the best latency balance. On PCIe setups, replication reduced cross-host traffic but pushed more dequant ops into CPU path (worse for small-batch latency).

Representative numbers (approx; runs on 4xA100 NVLink mesh, batch=1):
- Llama-2-70B MoE (top-1, 32k context): fp16 p95 = 820ms, int8 p95 = 720ms, mixed-FFN p95 = 700ms.
- Same model, PCIe-only machines: fp16 p95 = 860ms, int8 p95 = 1,020ms (degradation observed), mixed-FFN p95 = 835ms.
- Mistral-7B long-context (16k): fp16 p95 = 240ms, q4_0 p95 = 210ms, q4_0 + remote-expert (no replication) = 260ms.
- Qwen-14B (no MoE) attention-limited 64k: fp16 p95 = 1,560ms, q4_1 p95 = 1,420ms (10% improvement) — only when attention kernels are quant-capable.

Detailed observations and traces:
- Trace A (Llama MoE, nvlink): large memcpy spikes correspond to expert prefetch windows; quantized run reduced memcpy size by ~35% and shifted prefetch earlier (prefetch scheduler hit lower queue length), reducing tail.
- Trace B (Llama MoE, pcie-rack): observed multiple small synchronous memcpy calls after routing decision; dequant step performed on CPU pinned thread — causing CPU stalls and increasing host-to-device queueing.
- Kernel timelines show dequant kernels (host-side pack/unpack) can be as expensive as small FFN kernels when expert count per request is >1.

Root causes (analysis):
- Quantization reduces in-GPU memory footprint but introduces dequantization/packing cost. If that cost is off-path (CPU), latency wins are lost.
- Cross-device expert placement + lack of NVLink magnifies the cost of packing; synchronous memcpys become the dominant tail contributor for many small requests.
- Attention/KV-cache copy behavior for long-context workloads is still the largest consumer of memory bandwidth; if attention is not quantized (or kernels not optimized), the benefit from quantizing other parts is limited.

Operational mitigations we tested (and outcomes):
- Prefer replication for high-SLO MoE routes on PCIe racks (reduced remote fetches but higher memory) — works when customers accept reduced capacity density.
- Move dequantization to GPU (run quant-deq kernels on device) — significant wins when possible; in our prototyping it removed CPU stalls and recovered 60–80% of the int8 regression on PCIe.
- Kernel fusion: dequant + small FFN fused kernel improved throughput and tail by ~12% in microbenchmarks.
- Prefetch scheduling: push expert prefetch earlier based on routing heuristics to avoid synchronous memcpys during token generation. This helps on NVLink especially.
- Route-aware quantization selection: keep attention fp16 but FFN/emb quantized by default for long-context MoE workloads (best tradeoff).

Open questions / TODOs:
- Need more H100 runs: some int8 kernels are hardware-accelerated on H100; preliminary microbenchmarks show bigger wins but need full MoE routing end-to-end tests.
- Investigate zero-copy host staging (pinned buffers) for dequant path to reduce synchronous memcpy stalls on PCIe racks.
- Evaluate network-aware routing (prefer experts colocated with request origin) and measured effect on unit economics (capacity tradeoffs).
- Quantization-aware routing: does routing score change meaningfully when models are quantized (numerics)? Quick sanity checks show minimal change but need larger A/B evals.
- Explore compressed KV cache (lossless or low-loss) to reduce KV memcpy sizes for 32k/64k contexts.

Practical heuristics for runtime config (first-draft rules):
- If NVLink available and customers use 16k+ contexts: enable aggressive quantization (int8/AWQ) with replication=1–2 and move dequant to GPU.
- If PCIe-only and low-batch latency SLOs: prefer mixed-quant (FFN quantized, attention fp16) and replication=2 or colocate experts by default for latency-critical customers.
- For top-2 routing use-cases, prefer q4_1 or mixed-quant to avoid large dequant overheads; top-1 benefits more from int8.

Artifacts and reproducibility notes:
- Repro scripts: see linked PR /serving-runtime/pr/987 for the harness used. Profiling tags were added under trace tag: route-bandwidth-expt-2024-11.
- Experiment dir on GCS: gs://redwood-inference-experiments/routing-bandwidth-2024-11 (request access).

- [Diego] prototype GPU-side dequant kernels for our dequant pattern (PR scaffold exists).
- [Priya] run mixed-quant A/B on customer-like workloads (chat + search rerank) and report p95/p50 deltas.
- [Liam] investigate host pinned buffer zero-copy for PCIe racks and run microbench.

Notes / random observations (scratchpad):
- We saw one case where q4_0 produced worse numerics in router gating for tiny inputs; small follow-up needed (might be noise).
- Some kernel libs we linked are stale and don't support NVLink peer-to-peer memcpy optimizations; update list in confluence doc.
- User-facing guidance draft: "For best latency on multi-expert routes, prefer mixed quantization and enable device-side dequant if available."

References / links inserted inline: linked_artifacts above.

Unresolved: should we default to mixed-quant for all MoE models in hosted tier? risk: complexity for small customers vs big wins for long-context enterprise users. Recommendation: roll out as opt-in beta with telemetry for routing/kv memcpy times.

End of dump. This doc is intentionally informal — will convert into a short playbook if experiments (H100 + GPU dequant) confirm initial wins.
